deep.reconstruction:
Setting (from p.40): K is a finite combinatorial 1-complex (a graph). (D_i)_{i∈I} is a family of polygonal subcomplexes ('pseudolines', each a cycle) such that:
- every edge lies in exactly one D_i;
- two distinct D_i meet in at most one vertex;
- every vertex lies on at least two D_i.
This is a '1-dimensional arrangement of pseudolines'. ω is an extra 'orientation' datum, apparently introduced on p.40 through the small sub-arrangements K_I with |I|=3 and empty common intersection. Its exact nature is not legible here.

The page states the programme for showing that the 2-dimensional object can be recovered from (K,(D_i),ω). That object is the map ('carte') 𝒳: the cellular decomposition of the projective plane cut out by a pseudoline arrangement. Grothendieck invokes his 'general theorem on maps'. This is the combinatorial description of cellular embeddings of graphs in arbitrary, possibly non-orientable, surfaces. By it, it suffices to give two kinds of data:

(19) For each vertex s, a two-element set Z_s ⊂ Circ(A_s) consisting of two mutually inverse cyclic orders on the set A_s of darts (arcs) with origin s. A_s can be identified with the set of oriented pseudolines ±D_i through s, so |A_s| = 2ν_s ≥ 4. The degree hypothesis (≥4, 'suffit ≥3') ensures the two opposite cyclic orders are distinct, so Z_s is a genuine 2-element set, i.e. a local orientation torsor.

(20) For each dart a from s to s', a bijection ψ_a : Z_s → Z_s' (transport of local orientation along the edge), with (21) ψ_{reverse a} = ψ_a^{-1}.

'Canonical' means induced by the map 𝒳. Conversely, any such data satisfying (21) defines a cellular combinatorial embedding of K in some closed surface 𝒳, not necessarily the projective plane.

In modern terms this is a choice-free formulation of a 'general/signed rotation system' (embedding scheme). It uses a cyclic order up to reversal at each vertex plus edge signatures, packaged as a local system of Z/2-torsors on the graph, i.e. a principal Z/2-bundle with an equivariant rotation.

The next page adds two conditions that force the surface to be RP^2 and the D_i to be genuine pseudolines in it:
- (22) the antipodality condition ρ^{ν_s}(D_i) = -D_i: the pseudolines cross at s;
- (23) the Euler characteristic condition c0 - c1 + c2 = 1.
It then begins constructing the cyclic orders at s from the order in which lines through s meet a pseudoline not through s. The overall aim is a combinatorial reconstruction/characterization theorem for arrangements of pseudolines in the projective plane, from intersection-graph data plus a 'triple orientation' datum.
errors: No outright error. The converse is stated correctly with the explicit caveat that the resulting surface need not be the projective plane; this is handled on p.42 via (22) and the Euler characteristic condition.
Gap at this stage: how ω produces the canonical Z_s and ψ_a is not yet given. The construction only starts on the next page, so the page is a reduction, not a proof.
Minor: the degree hypothesis is written ambiguously ('≥4 (suffit ≥3)'). Degree ≥3 is what makes the two opposite cyclic orders distinct; in the arrangement every vertex has degree ≥4 anyway.

ideas.what: Encoding a cellular map on a possibly non-orientable surface by: at each vertex the 2-element set of opposite cyclic orders on darts, plus edge-transport bijections between these torsors, with ψ_{a^{-1}} = ψ_a^{-1}.
ideas.modern_name: generalized (signed) rotation system / embedding scheme; local-orientation Z/2-torsor formulation of non-orientable maps
ideas.usually_credited_to: Heffter–Edmonds (orientable case); Ringel, Youngs, Stahl (1978) and Mohar–Thomassen for non-orientable embedding schemes
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme (1984) discusses the theory of 'cartes' generally but not in this torsor form as far as I know

ideas.what: Reconstructing the 2-cell decomposition of RP^2 given by a pseudoline arrangement from purely 1-dimensional combinatorial data (graph partitioned into pseudoline cycles) plus orientation data on triples.
ideas.modern_name: combinatorial characterization of pseudoline arrangements; topological representation of rank-3 oriented matroids / chirotope reconstruction
ideas.usually_credited_to: Levi (1926), Folkman–Lawrence (1978), Goodman–Pollack (allowable sequences, 1980s), Björner–Las Vergnas–Sturmfels–White–Ziegler (1993)

ideas.what: Criterion that a combinatorial map built from the data is the projective plane: crossing (antipodality) condition at vertices plus Euler characteristic c0 - c1 + c2 = 1 (announced here, carried out on p.42).
ideas.modern_name: Euler characteristic test for cellular embeddings

missed.claim: Grothendieck treats pseudoline arrangements (the geometric side of rank-3 oriented matroids) inside his 'théorie des cartes', the same framework later developed as dessins d'enfants. He reduces the reconstruction of the arrangement to producing rotation/local-orientation data from 1-dimensional data plus a triple-orientation ω. This is a chirotope-like datum. The oriented matroid literature and the dessins/maps literature have essentially not been brought together in this way.
missed.quote: Par le théorème général des cartes, il suffit ... de construire, à partir de (K, 𝔇_{i∈I}, ω) ... Inversement ... on trouve une immersion cellulaire combinatoire de K dans une 𝒳 (peut-être pas le plan projectif !)
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It suggests viewing pseudoline arrangements, and possibly their realization spaces, as special maps/dessins. This could link Belyi-type and Galois actions on maps with stretchability questions for oriented matroids. The link is speculative, and the mathematics on this page itself is standard.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a reduction step: it invokes the general (non-orientable) rotation-system theorem in a nice choice-free torsor form, and the converse is correctly hedged. The content is standard combinatorial map theory. Its interest is historical: an independent Grothendieck treatment of pseudoline arrangements via 'cartes', parallel to oriented matroid theory.
transcription_corrections: '(l'inversion l'un de l'autre)' is the bracketed note under 'deux ordres circulaires', probably '(inverses l'un de l'autre)'.
'Z_s ⊂ A_s ↻_{A_s}' should be read as Z_s ⊂ Circ(A_s), the set of circular orders on A_s.
'𝔍_s' is probably '𝔇_s' (set of oriented pseudolines through s), with superscript D_i inserted above 'orientées'.
'construire [?] arithmétique' is more plausibly 'construire intrinsèquement des données'.
'Pour tout s∈S': 'tout' is struck through; likewise in 2°) 'tout sommet' is struck and replaced by 'arc a ∈ A'.
